newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end up on dlr rise, tame PPI hopes.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end up on dlr rise, tame PPI hopes.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries continued to rally Tuesday, as a higher dollar and hopes of market-friendly inflation and economic news this week pushed bond yields below the 6.50 percent level for the first time in nine months.
Bond prices jumped about three-quarters point to 100-23/32, while its yield fell six basis points to 6.45 percent -- its lowest closing level since March 6.
"The question is, 'how much further can this rally go?'" wondered Bruce Steinberg, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co.
Most market players agreed that there's still room for the market to rally further should economic data confirm the current low inflation-moderate growth scenario.

"In the short term, the market can rally at least 50 basis points," said Liz Miller, portfolio manager at Trevor, Stewart, Burton & Jacobsen Inc., explaining that "short term" means by year-end. She added that in 1995, both the economy and corporate earnings were stronger than in 1996, yet bond prices were lower last year.
"From a fundamental point of view, there's no reason we shouldn't be at same levels as last year," Miller said.
A year ago, the bond was holding around 6.28 percent.
And it was only two months ago the bond was above 7.0 percent.
"We've come a long way in a short time so consolidation needs to take place," Steinberg said. But "if the bond goes down much further, it's a powerful statement the Federal Reserve has to ease."

First, the market needs to be sure the Fed won't tighten anymore. The Fed's policy setting committee meets Wednesday, but economists are unanimous in forecasting no rate increases, with no rate moves seen through year end.

A Fed seemingly on hold for now helped propel Treasury prices higher Tuesday. A rise in the dollar against the mark, hope of market-friendly economic and inflation news this week and prospects of Democrats and Republicans finally meeting in order to continue budget deficit cuts were also cited as factors pushing up Treasuries.

After an early close Friday and a day off Monday, due to the Veterans Day holiday, Treasuries caught a bid in overseas trading during the night, which continued into the U.S. session. Traders said remarks by Bundesbank officials propped up the dollar, which led to foreign buying of Treasuries.

Early in the day, two Bundesbank officials said the current dollar-Deutsche mark of below 1.50 was inappropriate. Later, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said the dollar was on its way up, a move he welcomed. Late Tuesday, the dollar was at 1.5065 marks, up from 1.4945 marks Monday.

Meanwhile, the market was gearing up for a wave of key economic reports this week, beginning with the producer price index for October due Wednesday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. In a Reuters survey analysts forecast a 0.2 percent rise in the overall PPI and a 0.1 percent rise in the PPI excluding food and energy.

The market is also eying Thursday's data, which include the consumer price report and retail sales data for October. Players expect a 0.3 percent increase in both the overall and core CPI, and a rise in retail sales of no more than 0.5 percent.

"If we get those numbers, the market will continue to grind at the upper quadron of the range," said Kevin Sweeney, head government trader at CoreStates Capital Markets NA. He noted that there is "significant resistance" at around 6.40 percent, adding that a better than consensus number can push the bond below that level.

Sweeney said that most of the buying this session came from foreign buyers of five-year notes and higher, helped out bythe dollar's rise against the mark. "We've got to price in more than a stable Fed, but an accommodating Fed to drive yields lower on twos," he explained.

For now, analysts believe the bond will stick to a 6.25-6.50 percent range. "The economy is performing the way the market wants it to perform," Steinberg said. "To go beyond here suggests a weaker economy...It has slowed, but there's no recession. It's just correcting after excesses from first part of the year." -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867
